When two threads try to modify a standard java.util.HashMap simultaneously without proper synchronization, the underlying data structure enters an undefined, corrupted state. A HashMap is fundamentally not thread-safe. Its internal architecture relies on an array of Node buckets whose resizing, re-hashing, and structural modifications (such as put, remove, or clear) mutate internal pointers without atomic guarantees. If Thread A and Thread B concurrently write to the map, race conditions occur during bucket index calculation, collision resolution, and treeification transitions.

Historically, in pre-Java 8 implementations, concurrent modifications frequently triggered an infinite loop in the CPU during a resize operation due to cyclical linked-list pointer formation (a classic next-pointer corruption). Modern Java 8+ treeified HashMaps (where linked lists convert to red-black trees past a threshold) may not always loop infinitely, but they suffer from lost updates, array index out-of-bounds exceptions, ConcurrentModificationException (when fail-fast iterators detect structural changes, though this is best-effort and not a synchronization guarantee), and null-pointer dereferences within node pointers. The mutation of modCount is also non-atomic, meaning structural updates can overwrite each other, completely destroying data integrity.

items: Bucket Array Overwrite: When two threads evaluate the same initial capacity and load factor thresholds, they may simultaneously trigger a resize() operation, instantiating new arrays and abandoning or overwriting references initialized by the opposing thread.

ModCount Mutation Race: The modCount field tracks structural modifications for fail-fast iterators. Because incrementing modCount (modCount++) is not atomic (read-modify-write), concurrent updates result in lost increments, failing to catch concurrent mutations deterministically.

Red-Black Tree Corruption: In Java 8+, if concurrent insertions force treeification (TreeNode rotations), pointer adjustments in the tree roots and left/right child references become completely desynchronized, causing permanent traversal failures like infinite loops or missing keys.

parsed_answer.content: A common production trap is assuming that wrapping a HashMap inside Collections.synchronizedMap() makes it fully thread-safe for complex check-then-act sequences. While synchronizedMap synchronizes individual method calls, composite operations like 'if (!map.containsKey(k)) { map.put(k, v); }' are still prone to race conditions across multiple threads. Always use ConcurrentHashMap and atomic methods like putIfAbsent() for concurrent workloads.
